I am an avid Lubuntu user and am quite happy with it... but i want to try new things and learn as much as possible. So I've decided to try BSD out. I tried it in a virtual-box but the performance was horrible. I have an extra HDD sitting around so I will wipe it and install PC-BSD. I am most curious about the ZFS. I have used BTRFS and understand most of it, but I have heard ZFS can do all the same stuff and then some. I want to use a file system of this nature for protection from bit rot. I have lost data due to bit rot before and just want something immune to it. It is a pain it the ass to loose family photos to a single freaking bit. I understand that ZFS does check-summing and data duplication and think this might be what I am looking for. Will it work well with a single HDD or should I invest in multiple drives? Thanks for any info.
Looking to learn more about ZFS

I mirrored (RAID1) my Ubuntu 14.04 file server using ZFS about a year ago. I'd never used ZFS before so I spent some time doing test installs of various configurations until I felt comfortable with the technology and was sure how I wanted to configure it best for my needs. Since then I have had no need to re-visit it except to check the health of the drive array occasionally.

I am very happy with ZFS over a traditional hardware RAID solution. I've had RAID adapters go bad twice over the years and in both cases it was more luck than anything else that allowed us to get back up without any data loss. If I was running a data center that had high demand then I'd still go with a hardware solution, but for light demand or home ZFS is perfect.

I'm not sure if you can run it on a single drive, though I don't see why not. Performance would be shit though and you are completely exposed to drive failure, which is always my biggest concern. Long story short: buy at least 2 drives.

Just a note that RAID, whether s/w or h/w, is never a backup strategy. If those photos are important then back 'em up and store off-site. You could have the greatest RAID on the planet but it's still a single point of failure. RAID is a strategy for guaranteeing uptime and/or better disk performance, nothing more.
